author: Lucy Foley
title: Best Lucy Foley Books: Four Modern Thrillers Ranked
seoTitle: Best Lucy Foley Books: Thrillers Ranked | BestPickZone
description: Compare Lucy Foley's four modern standalone thrillers, from The Guest List to The Midnight Feast, with reading paths, honest tradeoffs and a Marple note.
introHtml:
The Guest List is the best Lucy Foley book for a first encounter with her contemporary thrillers. Its island wedding gives everyone a reason to be in the same place, behave badly and keep performing happiness. The Hunting Party is the colder, more insular alternative. The Paris Apartment swaps the group holiday for a suspicious building, while The Midnight Feast adds luxury-retreat satire and a stronger folk-horror flavor.

This is a ranking of those four modern standalone thrillers, not an exhaustive ranking of everything Foley has written. Her historical novels and her 2026 Miss Marple continuation, Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel, sit outside this comparison. There is a separate note on that newer mystery below so readers do not mistake a focused reading guide for a complete bibliography.

sections.heading: Your quickest route into Foley
sections.html:
• Best first read: The Guest List. Choose the wedding if you want a defined occasion, a shifting suspect list and plenty of social friction.
  • Best winter choice: The Hunting Party. Choose the reunion if isolation and long-established friendship roles interest you most.
  • Best change of setting: The Paris Apartment. Choose the building if you would rather follow an outsider trying to get answers.
  • Best for an extravagant setting: The Midnight Feast. Choose the retreat if expensive wellness and ominous woodland sound like a promising collision.

The ranking weighs how efficiently each setting generates suspicion, how distinct the experience feels and how easily a newcomer can settle into the structure. These are editorial preferences, not measured scores. None of these four novels requires another Foley book as preparation.

sections.heading: 1. The Guest List: the strongest overall introduction
sections.html:
Guests arrive on an Irish island for the wedding of Jules Keegan and Will Slater. Celebration turns into a murder mystery, and the weather helps keep the group together. That enclosed social setting is the essential starting point in HarperCollins' description.

The wedding is the reason this book leads the list. It naturally puts family, old friends and people with different levels of access to the couple into one room. There is an official story about the occasion, but each participant has a private reason to experience it differently. A seating arrangement, a speech or an old anecdote can become an assertion of power rather than harmless celebration.

That makes the multiple viewpoints useful. Instead of merely adding suspects, they change the meaning of behavior that another character takes for granted. The reader gets to notice the gap between the polished event and the relationships holding it together. The island makes leaving difficult; the wedding makes simply admitting unhappiness difficult.

The tradeoff: the story spends time establishing resentments before it delivers all the information a conventional detective novel would present near the beginning. Readers who want to inspect a crime scene immediately may feel held at a distance.

Skip this if: you dislike alternating narrators or want an investigation led by a professional detective. Start here for an ensemble under pressure, not a procedural.

sections.heading: 2. The Hunting Party: best for winter isolation
sections.html:
A group of old university friends meets for a New Year gathering in the Scottish Highlands. The remote setting and deteriorating conditions turn a ritual reunion into a much more threatening experience. Foley's official bookshelf identifies the Oxford-friends setup; the publisher's title page confirms the book and its isolated-country-house approach.

The Hunting Party works especially well if you recognize the discomfort of returning to a group that still expects everyone to play an old role. The person who once dominated a room may assume that position is permanent. Someone else's achievement can disturb the group more than an open argument. Those tensions give the remoteness something to amplify.

It ranks just below The Guest List because the friendship circle is narrower and more repetitive by design. That can create delicious claustrophobia, but it also means you must want to spend time with this particular social dynamic. The wedding gives the first-ranked book more types of relationships to bring into collision.

Choose this one when you want weather, distance and uncomfortable intimacy to matter as much as the question of guilt. The pleasure comes from watching the group's apparently familiar arrangement become harder to maintain.

Skip this if: privileged friends being cruel to each other is already a worn-out premise for you. A remote setting does not make an abrasive cast comforting company.

sections.heading: 3. The Paris Apartment: best for outsider suspicion
sections.html:
A missing resident draws attention to an apartment building where the people behind the other doors have reasons to be guarded. The publisher's synopsis foregrounds the building's concealed lives rather than presenting Paris as a sightseeing destination.

This is the best pivot after one of the holiday thrillers. A neighborhood can be crowded while an individual still lacks information, allies or access. Here, the structure of the building makes proximity unsettling: being close enough to hear or see something is different from being willing to explain it. Doors and shared spaces become boundaries between competing versions of events.

The setting also changes the reader's role. Instead of arriving with a group whose grievances gradually emerge, you are invited to treat the residents' daily arrangements as a problem to decode. That produces a more exploratory reading experience, with suspicion attaching to who knows whom and what they will acknowledge.

It sits third because the atmosphere is stronger as a reason to choose it than any promise of a perfectly transparent puzzle. Readers who dislike information being parceled out across several perspectives may find the accumulation of secrets conspicuous. For someone tired of another remote weekend, however, it may be the most appealing Foley starting point.

Skip this if: you want a romantic Paris escape or a single narrator who can give you a steady account from start to finish. This is a city viewed through mistrust.

sections.heading: 4. The Midnight Feast: best for luxury with an ominous edge
sections.html:
The opening of an expensive countryside retreat brings guests into a setting shadowed by an ancient wood and a past that the polished new venue cannot simply erase. Foley's official description establishes the opening-weekend setup and the mix of old friends and enemies.

The distinctive attraction is the mismatch between the experience being sold and the place underneath it. A luxury retreat promises to control atmosphere: the food, the setting, the feeling that every need has been anticipated. Suspense comes easily when that promise starts to look like a way of excluding inconvenient people and stories.

This is the choice for readers who want Foley to push the scenery and symbolism harder. The woodland associations make the threat feel less limited to a disagreement at dinner, while the retreat gives the social antagonism a more deliberately extravagant stage. Its appeal is partly theatrical, so choose it for that richness rather than expect the relatively stripped-down chill of The Hunting Party.

Fourth place reflects its narrower fit. If you want a disciplined weekend mystery with little tonal decoration, the earlier books are easier recommendations. If you enjoy an uneasy overlap between upscale hospitality and folk-horror imagery, move this one above The Paris Apartment.

Skip this if: you prefer a restrained closed-circle mystery to folklore-inflected spectacle.

sections.heading: The new Miss Marple book belongs on a separate track
sections.html:
Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel is a 2026 Lucy Foley novel featuring Agatha Christie's Miss Marple. The official Christie site places the mystery in a Swiss hotel and describes a death connected with a gondola journey. This is a new continuation written by Foley, not a rediscovered Christie manuscript.

It is worth distinguishing because a recognizable detective changes the reading promise. Someone seeking a Miss Marple mystery is bringing expectations about observation and investigation that differ from approaching an entirely new Foley ensemble. It is therefore acknowledged here rather than assigned a speculative position in the four-book comparison.

If that detective is the main reason for your interest, start your shopping comparison with the Marple book. If you want to understand Foley's contemporary standalone style first, choose The Guest List. Her historical fiction is a separate path again; the publisher's author catalog lists those titles alongside the mysteries without making them part of one series.

sections.heading: How to avoid choosing the wrong Foley book
sections.html:
The most useful question is what kind of group do you want to be trapped with? A wedding combines people who have different claims on the hosts. A reunion traps people inside their own shared history. An apartment building produces uneasy contact between neighbors. A luxury retreat puts the people buying an experience beside the people and places that make it possible.

For a concrete example, choose The Guest List for a reading group that enjoys comparing how different narrators understand the same event. Choose The Hunting Party for a winter read where the enclosed setting is the priority. Choose The Paris Apartment if a missing-person inquiry sounds more appealing than an event waiting to go wrong. Choose The Midnight Feast when the setting itself should feel overripe with threat.

Do not confuse short chapters or changing narrators with continuous action. Foley often builds suspense by withholding context and moving the reader between people. That can be compulsive for someone who enjoys comparison, but frustrating for someone who wants to remain beside one investigator and follow every step.

sections.heading: Start here; skip this first
sections.html:
Read The Guest List first for the clearest combination of social occasion, enclosed setting and shifting suspicion. Choose The Hunting Party instead if wintry atmosphere is your deciding factor. Save The Midnight Feast until you know you enjoy a more heightened presentation, unless its particular setting is what attracted you in the first place.

You can read the four ranked books in any order. For a different style of twist-driven suspense, compare our Alex Michaelides recommendations. For alternatives beyond one author, browse psychological thrillers and the author-guide hub.
